title: The two sons
hook: one brother's offering is accepted, the other kills him, and a crow shows him how to bury the body (5:27–31)
carry: one life is like all lives

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawbah, turning back. Adam's words were your line: we wronged ourselves; forgive us. Did you skip an explanation and just say so? Day twenty-eight.

This week, the first human story. A steward announced, and the angels asking why. The names. The one who wouldn't bow. A garden with one tree. A whisper. And a way back. All of it happened between God and the first two people. Now the story leaves the garden and comes down to earth, and the very next thing it shows us is a family. Two brothers. Sibling rivalry has its classics: who got the bigger slice, who Mom liked better, who got the car. And this time, the rivalry doesn't end in a slammed door. It ends in the first death in the human story.
screen: `A WEEK IN THE FIRST STORY.` → `DOWN TO EARTH: A FAMILY.` → `TWO BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Surah five tells it, and calls them simply the two sons of Adam. It never names them; tradition calls them Qabil and Habil, Cain and Abel. Each brings an offering to God. One is accepted. The other isn't. And the one whose offering was refused says: I will kill you. His brother's answer, in Pickthall's words: “Allah accepteth only from those who ward off (evil).” In other words: it isn't about me. Look at your own heart. Then he says more. Even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won't raise mine to kill you; I fear God. And his brother kills him anyway. Then comes the strangest, saddest detail. The killer stands over the body and doesn't know what to do. God sends a crow, scratching at the ground, to show him how to hide his brother's body. And he cries out: woe to me, can't I even be like this crow? And he's filled with regret. Right after this story comes a line addressed to the Children of Israel. Whoever kills a soul, except in justice, it's as if he killed all people, and in Pickthall's words, “whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.” Jewish readers will recognize a close teaching in the Mishnah. A hadith in Bukhari adds: for every unjust killing since, a share falls on that first son, because he was the first to do it. So the lesson of this first family is simple and enormous. One person is a whole world.
screen: `TWO OFFERINGS, ONE ACCEPTED.` · `I WON'T RAISE MY HAND.` · `A CROW, SCRATCHING THE GROUND.` · `ONE LIFE, ALL MANKIND.` · then, large: `ONE LIFE IS LIKE ALL LIVES.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Let a jealousy come to mind, one you've carried for a while. A sibling, a friend, a colleague, someone who seemed to get what you wanted. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just sit next to it. Notice where it lives in your body. Then picture the other person as a whole world: their own worries, their own sleepless nights, people who love them. Hold that for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Habil, the brother whose offering was accepted and who told Qabil it isn't about me, look at your own heart, before the first death in the human story.
Your line: one life is like all lives. Today, treat one person you'd usually hurry past as if they were a whole world. A week, done. Day twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 28 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NINE HUNDRED AND FIFTY YEARS.`

howItsDone: Muslims often cite 5:32 to teach the sanctity of every human life, and it appears in sermons and statements against violence; the story of the two sons is taught as a warning about jealousy.

fork.setup: your brother, furious that God accepted your offering and not his, says: I will kill you. what do you answer?
options: even if you raise your hand, I won't raise mine.
fork.reveal: God accepts only from those who guard against evil, he says, and he won't raise his hand. the story honors him for it.

original.note: Arabic: "the two sons of Adam," the Qur'an's only name for them in 5:27.

trapdoor: what you thought: Cain and Abel, a Bible story.
what it means: the two sons — Muslims know the story too, from surah five: an offering refused, a brother who won't fight back, a crow, and a verse about every life.
what a scholar hears: 5:32 is addressed to the Children of Israel and echoes a teaching in the Mishnah; a hadith in Bukhari says a share of every unjust killing falls on the first son, who began it.
